meta.description: What Meta Muse means for creators, what DTC brands should tell them, how to label posts, and a ready-made brief and creator pack to send today.

hero.title: What DTC brands should tell their creators about Meta Muse
paragraphs: What should a DTC brand tell its creators about Meta's Muse? That it could be good news for honest, useful posts. Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, which Meta launched in the UK in November 2026 after a September launch in North America, and it can work from the Reels people save on Instagram, so a post saved today could help someone buy weeks later.

Ask your creators to keep their own voice, show real-life fit, and keep their code, link and ad label on every post. This guide gives the reasons, the labelling rules, a message to paste and a pack to send.

sections.heading: Why does Muse matter for creators and influencers?

blocks.html: Muse can carry a creator's recommendation to the point of purchase, and shoppers want creator voices in AI answers. In IAB's survey of people who use AI for shopping research, Gen Z rated creator reviews in AI recommendations nearly as influential as brand information (27% against 29%), and half of Gen Z and Millennials have discovered creators through AI. The same study found the UK the most cautious Western market.

Muse also does the comparison work, picking mainly on price and stock, so a post that only lists specs adds little. Real-life fit, such as the size chosen or how a product holds up after a week, gives shoppers a reason to save and come back. Price, stock and returns are the brand's job: see how to change your creator programme for Muse.
Almost nothing about how they create. The small changes: name the product, show it in real life, answer one buying question, and include the code and link.

Creators should not write for AI. Muse works from posts shoppers chose to save, and a scripted or keyword-stuffed post gives people little reason to save it. Fake reviews and hidden ad labels damage the same trust; the ASA expects a prominent "ad" label upfront.

sections.heading: How should creators label posts now?

blocks.html: Label every post involving a gift, payment, code or affiliate link as an ad, clearly and at the start. Muse changes none of the UK or FTC's US rules.

head: UK (ASA)
US (FTC)
rows: Posts with an affiliate link or code, or after any payment or incentive, even an unsolicited gift
Any financial, employment, personal or family relationship with a brand, including free or discounted products
A prominent "ad" label upfront; "Gifted" alone is unlikely to be enough
In videos, disclose in the video itself, not only the description

blocks.html: The ASA holds brands and influencers both responsible for making ads identifiable, and brands and affiliates jointly responsible for affiliate-link ads.

sections.heading: How could creators earn more from Muse?

blocks.html: By putting their code and link on every post, posting more than once and moving up a reward ladder you set.

Instagram told TechCrunch that links on creators' Reels draw about twice the clicks of links in bio, but its shoppable Reels rollout does not yet name the UK, so UK creators should keep codes in captions and on screen.
A clear ladder keeps creators going:

items: On joining: free product.
First sale: commission or a flat fee.
Regular posting: more product.
Consistent sales and posts: a higher commission tier.
Top creators: a closer role, such as an ambassador place.

blocks.html: For subscriptions, the low first order motivates no one, so pay a flat fee per sale or commission on renewals. More in how to keep creators for the long term.

sections.heading: What can you send your creators this week?

blocks.html: A short, warm note from a named person on your team, like this one:

items: Hi [first name],

A quick note about Muse, Meta's new personal AI agent, live in the US and Canada since September and now in the UK. People can connect Instagram to it, and it can act on Reels they've saved, like turning a saved recipe into a shopping list. It also remembers what people like and makes suggestions. That's good news for honest, useful posts like yours: a post saved today could help someone choose weeks from now.
You don't need to change how you create, but a few habits help:
- Say [product] clearly and show how it fits into your life.
- Answer a question a buyer would ask, like [buying question].
- Start your caption with "Ad" and say it in the video too.
- Add your code [code] and link [link] to every post.
Thanks for being part of [Brand].
[Your name]

sections.heading: What should go in a Muse creator pack?

blocks.html: Four parts: the message above, content prompts, caption and on-camera lines, and the per-post checklist. Add your product, code and link, and send it with every product.

sections.heading: Which content prompts can creators use with their audience?
sections.eyebrow: What should go in a Muse creator pack?

items: Answer your followers' top question about [product] in under 30 seconds, naming it out loud.
Open your first box of [product] on camera: what is inside and what surprised you.
Show how [product] fits, on you or in your space, and which size you chose and why.
Walk through your routine and show where [product] fits in your day.
Show how you did it before [product], how you do it now, and what changed.
Show [product] before and after use, describing only what you saw.
Make a "save this for later" list of three things you'd tell a friend before they buy [product].
Show Muse at work: save a recipe Reel and ask Muse to turn it into a shopping list.
Tell followers that saved posts stay ready for when they buy, and Muse can work from them if they connect Instagram.

sections.heading: Which lines can creators use in captions or on camera?
sections.eyebrow: What should go in a Muse creator pack?

items: "Save this for when you're ready to buy."
"If you've connected Instagram to Muse, your saved posts can help it build your list."
"My code [code] is in the caption."
"Ad: [Brand] sent me this to try."

sections.heading: What should brands not ask creators to say?
sections.eyebrow: What should go in a Muse creator pack?

blocks.html: Don't script product claims, and don't ask creators to say Muse will recommend them, since nothing confirms it. Never ask them to drop or soften the ad label or to stuff captions with keywords.

sections.heading: What should creators check before every post?

blocks.html: Six quick checks:

items: I have used the product and give my own view.
I name the product and show it in real life.
The post answers one buyer question.
"Ad" starts my caption and is said or shown in the video.
My code and link are in the caption, and on screen where possible.
I have not changed my style for an algorithm or an AI.

sections.heading: Where do we think this is heading?

blocks.html: Neither of these is a confirmed Muse feature, but creators should be ready for both.

Muse will amplify the creators people already trust. Saves start with creators, so we expect Muse to lean on them rather than replace them. If Meta's plans to credit creators reach Muse, trusted creators gain the most.

Creator codes could become a new link in bio. If shopping agents surface older posts and their codes, a review could earn commission for months. Nothing confirms Muse uses creator codes, and a Tom's Guide test of its coupon finding came back untrustworthy or empty. A code on every post leaves creators ready.

sections.heading: What other questions do buyers ask?

items.title: Do creators need to mention Muse in their posts?
items.body: No. What matters most is a post worth saving, with the product in real life and an honest view.

items.title: Will Muse replace influencers?
items.body: No sign of it: Meta says more than half of consumers say creators influence their shopping. Muse takes on comparison, and creators make the posts shoppers save.

items.title: Does Muse pay creators?
items.body: No evidence says so: Digiday reported Meta's position that Muse carries no ads, and Meta has announced no creator payments. Commission comes through the creator's own code and link.
